parsed_answer.content: In the context of high-scale distributed systems, SLIs, SLOs, and SLAs form the bedrock of Site Reliability Engineering (SRE). An SLI (Service Level Indicator) is a quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service provided, such as request latency or error rate. It is the raw data point—the 'what' we are measuring. An SLO (Service Level Objective) is a target value or range of values for a service level that is measured by an SLI; it represents the 'goal' we strive to hit to keep our users happy. An SLA (Service Level Agreement) is the final layer: a legal or business contract between a service provider and a customer that defines the consequences—usually financial penalties or service credits—if the SLOs are consistently missed. While SLIs and SLOs are internal operational tools used to drive engineering decisions, the SLA is an external-facing promise that dictates the business risk of downtime.

items: SLIs are typically derived from metrics captured at the edge or via instrumentation (e.g., Micrometer/Prometheus counters). A common SLI is the ratio of successful HTTP 2xx responses to total requests.

SLOs are often expressed as a percentage over a rolling window (e.g., 99.9% availability over 30 days). This window allows for an 'Error Budget', which is the remaining margin of failure allowed before the SLO is breached.

When an Error Budget is exhausted, SRE teams typically halt new feature deployments to focus exclusively on stability, ensuring the system returns to a healthy state before resuming the feature velocity.

SLAs are rarely as strict as SLOs. For instance, an internal SLO might be 99.95% availability, while the customer-facing SLA might only promise 99.0% to provide a buffer for maintenance and unexpected outages.

parsed_answer.content: Senior trap: Never set your SLOs to 100%. A 100% availability target is mathematically impossible in distributed systems and operationally toxic. Always aim for a realistic 'nines' target (e.g., 99.9%) and ensure your SLA is always lower than your SLO to prevent paying out credits for minor, non-critical blips that your internal monitoring caught early.

title: What are SLIs, SLOs, and SLAs?
